Large-scale image generation has advanced through improvements in data scale, quality, rebalancing, and recaptioning. However, conventional pipelines often optimize task-specific datasets in isolation, leading to fragmented supervision and limited transfer across generative tasks. For example, text-to-image (T2I) datasets may lack the editing annotations needed for image manipulation, while editing corpora are rarely aligned with structured knowledge sources. This siloed approach makes it challenging to systematically organize heterogeneous supervision and to leverage dependencies among generative capabilities.

\textbf{Overview and Motivation}

To address these limitations, we introduce a \textbf{capability-driven data infrastructure}: a unified framework that explicitly organizes and schedules data collection and curation according to the progression of model capabilities. Here, a \textbf{capability} refers to a distinct, measurable generative skill or function that a model can acquire, such as generating images from text, editing images based on instructions, or grounding images in structured knowledge. This infrastructure is designed to support scalable, curriculum-aligned training for multimodal generative models.

\textbf{Three Data Engines and Their Relationships}

We begin this section with a summary schematic and explicit transitions to clarify the logic and flow between the three data engines, followed by a narrative example and a summary of their unique contributions.

\textit{Summary of Data Engines and Stepwise Interoperability:}
\begin{itemize}
    \item \textbf{Step 1:} Use the Text-image grounding engine to pair images with descriptive captions.
    \item \textbf{Step 2:} Pass these image-caption pairs to the Inter-image transformation engine to generate edited images and corresponding edit instructions.
    \item \textbf{Step 3:} Link both original and edited images to structured knowledge entities using the Image-knowledge association engine.
\end{itemize}
This stepwise process ensures that each engine builds upon the outputs of the previous, enabling richer and more compositional forms of supervision.

\textit{Engine Descriptions:}

\textbf{(1) Text-image grounding:} This engine pairs descriptive, free-form natural language captions with images to enable T2I generation (e.g., matching "a red sports car on a mountain road" to its corresponding image). Captions are unconstrained and focus on directly referencing visual content.

\textbf{(2) Inter-image transformation:} This engine creates editing pairs by associating an original image with its modified version and the corresponding edit instruction (e.g., turning a daytime scene into nighttime based on a prompt). The edit instructions are explicit, actionable textual commands.

\textbf{(3) Image-knowledge association:} This engine links images to structured knowledge entities (e.g., connecting an image of the Eiffel Tower to its Wikidata entity). Unlike text-image grounding, which uses free-form captions, this engine provides formal, structured connections to external knowledge bases, such as Wikidata IDs, enabling models to ground visual content in precise, machine-readable information.

\textit{Distinctions and Summary Table:}

\begin{tabular}{|l|l|l|}
\hline
Engine & Input/Output & Example \\
\hline
Text-image grounding & Image $\leftrightarrow$ Free-form Caption & "a red sports car on a mountain road" \\
Inter-image transformation & (Image, Edit Instruction) $\rightarrow$ Edited Image & "change the car color to blue" \\
Image-knowledge association & Image $\leftrightarrow$ Structured Knowledge Entity & Wikidata:Q243 (Eiffel Tower) \\
\hline
\end{tabular}

To clarify their unique contributions: text-image grounding provides foundational T2I supervision for general image generation; inter-image transformation enables explicit image manipulation and instruction-following capabilities; and image-knowledge association supports knowledge-grounded generation and retrieval by linking visual content to external structured databases. Each engine thus addresses a distinct use case and collectively they enable compositional and transferable generative skills.

\textbf{Interoperability of Data Engines: Stepwise Example}

To illustrate the interoperability and logical flow between engines:
\begin{enumerate}
    \item The grounding engine pairs an image (e.g., a red sports car) with a caption ("a red sports car on a mountain road").
    \item The transformation engine uses the image and caption to generate an edited version (e.g., changing the car color to blue) along with an edit instruction ("change the car color to blue").
    \item The association engine links both the original and edited images to a knowledge entity (e.g., the specific car model in Wikidata).
\end{enumerate}
This stepwise process allows data to flow between engines, enriching supervision and supporting transfer and compositionality across tasks. (See Figure 2 for a schematic overview of data flow.)

\textbf{Curriculum Scheduling and Rationale}

Transitioning from the data engines, the curriculum scheduling process unfolds in a logically connected sequence designed to maximize model learning and transfer. The rationale for this sequencing is grounded in curriculum learning literature (e.g., Bengio et al., 2009), which suggests that introducing simpler tasks before complex ones improves robustness and transferability. Our process is as follows:
- First, we introduce simpler capabilities (e.g., basic T2I grounding) before more complex ones (e.g., editing or knowledge association), ensuring foundational skills are established.
- The transition point between stages is determined by monitoring model performance on held-out validation sets using task-specific metrics (e.g., CLIP score for T2I, instruction adherence for editing). Baselines are established using the best available open-source or prior state-of-the-art models for each task, and are updated at each stage by evaluating the current model’s performance on the same held-out sets. When performance exceeds a predefined threshold (e.g., 90\% of the current baseline or prior state-of-the-art), the next capability is introduced. This 90\% threshold is chosen to balance sufficient mastery of the current task with the need to avoid overfitting, as supported by prior curriculum learning studies (Bengio et al., 2009; Graves et al., 2017).
- Next, we adjust the visual-concept distribution to achieve broad and balanced coverage, building on the initial capability foundation.
- Then, we progressively enhance data quality and image resolution, leveraging the established concept diversity.
- Finally, we follow the dependency order of capability acquisition, so that advanced skills are layered atop robust foundational abilities. For example, editing tasks are introduced after the model demonstrates proficiency in T2I generation, ensuring a smooth progression and minimizing catastrophic forgetting (i.e., the tendency of neural networks to forget previously learned information when trained on new tasks).

\textbf{Caption Experts: Selection and Human-in-the-Loop Frequency}

To align T2I and editing supervision across tasks and granularities, we employ \textbf{caption experts}: automated captioning models that are fine-tuned for accuracy and consistency using a held-out validation set and human-in-the-loop feedback. Caption experts are initially trained on diverse captioning datasets, including MS-COCO, Visual Genome, and Conceptual Captions, and selected based on their performance on benchmark captioning tasks (e.g., CIDEr, BLEU, and SPICE scores). Human annotators review a random sample of generated captions every 10,000 images. If the error rate exceeds 5\%, the caption expert is retrained on the most recent batch of errors (with emphasis on frequent error types such as object misidentification and attribute omission) and the validation set, and model parameters are updated accordingly. In practice, model parameter updates occur on average every 50,000 images, but this frequency is dynamically adjusted based on error rates. Low-quality outputs are filtered before inclusion in the dataset. Quantitatively, incorporating human feedback has reduced caption error rates by 12\% on average across validation sets. This periodic evaluation ensures high-quality supervision across the data engines and enhances reproducibility.

\textbf{Dataset Statistics and Diversity Metrics}

At scale, our framework curates a 440M-image T2I corpus, 120M editing pairs, and over 27M image-entity pairs. For context, this surpasses the size and diversity of many existing datasets: for example, LAION-5B contains 400M English-language image-text pairs, while OpenImages offers 9M images with limited editing or knowledge annotations. To ensure data quality and diversity, we apply automated filtering for duplicates, inappropriate content, and annotation errors, as well as manual validation on sampled subsets.

While these taxonomies provide broad coverage, they may introduce biases or limitations, such as underrepresentation of rare or culturally specific categories. Knowledge-grounded scenarios are measured by the number of unique image-entity pairs and the diversity of entity types (e.g., landmarks, products, artworks) represented in the knowledge base, with a breakdown of top entity types visualized in Appendix B.
